question: According to the manual, why do you look for hazards well before they become emergencies?
choice_a: So you have time to plan a way out of any emergency that develops
choice_b: So you can report them to the DMV later
choice_c: So you can avoid checking your mirrors
choice_d: So you can maintain a constant speed regardless of conditions
explanation: The manual states you look for hazards in order to have time to plan a way out of any emergency, making you a prepared, defensive driver.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-21

question: How does the manual define a "driver distraction"?
choice_a: A mechanical malfunction in the vehicle
choice_b: Any activity performed while the vehicle is legally parked
choice_c: Only the use of a cell phone while driving
choice_d: Anything that takes your attention away from driving
explanation: The manual defines a driver distraction as anything that takes your attention away from driving, putting yourself, passengers, other vehicles, and pedestrians in danger.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-21

question: According to the Large Truck Crash Causation Study (LTCCS) cited in the manual, what percentage of large-truck crashes occurred when the CMV driver was externally distracted?
choice_a: 2 percent
choice_b: 5 percent
choice_d: 15 percent
explanation: The LTCCS reported that 8 percent of large-truck crashes occurred when CMV drivers were externally distracted, compared to 2 percent when internally distracted.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-21

question: Research cited in the manual found that talking on a cell phone, even hands-free, saps the brain of what percentage of the energy it would ordinarily devote to safe driving?
explanation: The manual cites NHTSA research showing the burden of talking on a cell phone, even hands-free, saps the brain of 39% of the energy it would ordinarily devote to safe driving.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-21

question: Under the Federal restriction on hand-held mobile phone use described in the manual, what is the CDL disqualification period for a second conviction within 3 years?
choice_a: 60 days
choice_b: 30 days
choice_d: 120 days
explanation: The manual states disqualification is 60 days for the second offense within 3 years and 120 days for three or more offenses within 3 years, along with civil penalties up to $2,750.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-22

question: Research cited in the manual found that the odds of a safety-critical event are how many times greater for CMV drivers who dial a mobile telephone while driving compared to those who do not?
choice_a: 2 times
choice_b: 6 times
choice_d: 23.2 times
explanation: The manual states the odds of a safety-critical event are 6 times greater for CMV drivers who dial a mobile phone while driving; dialing drivers averaged 3.8 seconds with eyes off the roadway.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-22

question: The manual states that sending or receiving a text message takes a driver's eyes off the road for an average of how long, during which a vehicle at 55 mph would travel about the length of a football field?
choice_a: 1.5 seconds
choice_b: 2.8 seconds
choice_d: 4.6 seconds
explanation: The manual states texting takes your eyes off the road for an average of 4.6 seconds, during which you would travel 371 feet at 55 mph, roughly the length of a football field.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-23

question: According to the manual, what happens to crash rates if drivers react a half-second slower because of distractions?
choice_a: Crash rates double
choice_b: Crash rates stay the same
choice_d: Crash rates triple
explanation: The manual states, "If drivers react a half-second slower because of distractions, crashes double."
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-23

question: How does the manual define "road rage," distinguishing it from aggressive driving?
choice_a: Driving faster than the posted speed limit
choice_b: Driving slowly in the left lane
choice_d: Operating a motor vehicle with the intent of doing harm to others or physically assaulting a driver or their vehicle
explanation: The manual defines road rage as operating a motor vehicle with the intent of doing harm to others or physically assaulting a driver or their vehicle, whereas aggressive driving is described as operating in a selfish, bold, or pushy manner without regard for others' rights or safety.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-23

question: What does the manual say you should do first and foremost when confronted by an aggressive driver?
choice_a: Make every attempt to get out of their way
choice_b: Speed up to hold your position in the travel lane
choice_c: Make eye contact to show confidence
choice_d: Flash your high beams as a warning
explanation: The manual states that first and foremost, you should make every attempt to get out of an aggressive driver's way, put your pride aside, avoid eye contact, and ignore gestures.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-24

question: Why does the manual say you are at greater risk when driving at night?
choice_a: Traffic volume is always heavier at night
choice_b: Speed limits are higher after dark
choice_c: Vehicles are required to travel closer together
choice_d: Drivers can't see hazards as quickly as in daylight, so they have less time to respond
explanation: The manual explains that at night, drivers can't see hazards as quickly as in daylight, so they have less time to respond and are less able to avoid a crash if caught by surprise.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-24

question: Why does the manual advise against using dark or tinted corrective lenses when driving at night?
choice_a: They cut down the light you need to see clearly under night driving conditions
choice_b: They are more expensive to replace
choice_c: They are prohibited by insurance policies
choice_d: They interfere with dashboard gauge lighting
explanation: The manual warns that tinted lenses cut down the light needed to see clearly at night, even though a driver might think they help with glare.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-25

question: The manual states that even two seconds of glare blindness can be dangerous because a vehicle traveling 55 mph will cover approximately what distance during that time?
choice_a: A few feet
choice_b: 10 feet
choice_c: More than half the distance of a football field
choice_d: About one mile
explanation: The manual states that even two seconds of glare blindness can be dangerous, since a vehicle going 55 mph will travel more than half the distance of a football field during that time.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-25

question: A congressionally mandated study of 80 long-haul truck drivers cited in the manual found that drivers averaged how much sleep per day?
choice_a: Less than 5 hours
choice_b: 6 to 7 hours
choice_d: More than 9 hours
explanation: The manual cites a Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration study finding that long-haul truck drivers averaged less than 5 hours of sleep per day.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-25

question: To maintain alertness on long trips, the manual recommends taking periodic breaks about how often?
choice_a: Every 25 miles or 30 minutes
choice_b: Every 100 miles or 2 hours
choice_d: Only when refueling
explanation: The manual advises taking periodic breaks about every 100 miles or 2 hours during long trips to help maintain alertness.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-26

question: According to the manual, approximately how far ahead can you see at night with low-beam headlights, compared to high beams?
choice_a: Low beams about 100 feet; high beams about 200 feet
choice_b: Low beams and high beams provide the same visibility
choice_c: Low beams about 500 feet; high beams about 800 feet
choice_d: Low beams about 250 feet; high beams about 350-500 feet
explanation: The manual states that with low beams you can see ahead about 250 feet, and with high beams about 350-500 feet, and you must adjust speed to keep stopping distance within your sight distance.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-26

question: What does the manual say is the best advice for driving in fog?
choice_a: Use your high beams to see further ahead
choice_b: Speed up to get through the fog bank quickly
choice_c: Don't drive; pull off the road into a rest area or truck stop until visibility improves
choice_d: Follow closely behind another vehicle's taillights
explanation: The manual states, "The best advice for driving in fog is don't," recommending drivers pull off the road into a rest area or truck stop until visibility is better.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-27

question: According to the manual, what is the minimum tread depth required in every major groove on front tires?
choice_a: 1/32 inch
choice_b: 2/32 inch
choice_d: 8/32 inch
explanation: The manual states you must have at least 4/32 inch tread depth in every major groove on front tires, and at least 2/32 inch on other tires, which is especially important in winter conditions.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-28

question: If a tire becomes too hot to touch during very hot weather driving, what does the manual say you should do about air pressure?
choice_a: Let air out to bring the pressure back to normal
choice_b: Add air to compensate for the heat
choice_c: Do not let air out; remain stopped until the tire cools off
choice_d: Switch to a spare tire immediately regardless of pressure
explanation: The manual instructs drivers not to let air out of hot tires, since the pressure will then be too low once the tires cool, and to remain stopped until an overly hot tire cools off or it may blow out or catch fire.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-29

question: How does the manual define a "passive" railroad-highway crossing?
choice_a: One with no traffic control device, where the decision to stop or proceed rests entirely with the driver
choice_b: One equipped with flashing red lights and gates
choice_c: One found only on interstate highways
choice_d: One that is permanently closed to commercial traffic
explanation: The manual defines a passive crossing as one without any type of traffic control device, requiring the driver to recognize the crossing, search for a train, and decide if there is sufficient clear space to cross safely.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-30

question: If there is no white stop line painted on the pavement at a railroad crossing, the manual states that vehicles required to stop must stop no closer than how many feet from the nearest rail?
choice_a: 5 feet
choice_b: 15 feet
choice_d: 50 feet
explanation: The manual states vehicles required to stop at a cross-buck sign must stop no closer than 15 feet nor more than 50 feet from the nearest rail of the nearest track when there is no white stop line.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-30

question: According to the manual, how long does it take a typical tractor-trailer unit to clear a double track?
choice_a: At least 5 seconds
choice_b: At least 10 seconds
choice_d: More than 30 seconds
explanation: The manual states it takes a typical tractor-trailer unit at least 14 seconds to clear a single track and more than 15 seconds to clear a double track.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-31

question: What does the manual instruct you to do with the transmission before starting down a long, steep downgrade?
choice_a: Shift into neutral to conserve fuel
choice_b: Wait until speed builds up, then downshift
choice_c: Shift the transmission to a low gear before starting down the grade
choice_d: Keep the transmission in the highest available gear
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to shift the transmission to a low gear before starting down the grade, warning that trying to downshift after speed has already built up may make it impossible to get into a lower gear at all.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-32

question: According to the manual, how do escape ramps built on steep mountain downgrades stop a runaway vehicle?
choice_a: By automatically triggering the vehicle's air brakes
choice_b: By using a long bed of loose, soft material to slow the vehicle
choice_c: By using a series of speed bumps
choice_d: By using an electronic barrier gate
explanation: The manual states escape ramps use a long bed of loose, soft material to slow a runaway vehicle, sometimes in combination with an upgrade, and are usually located a few miles from the top of the downgrade.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-33

question: In an emergency where you don't have enough room to stop, what does the manual say about steering compared to braking?
choice_a: You should always brake rather than attempt to steer around an obstacle
choice_b: Steering to avoid an obstacle is illegal in a commercial vehicle
choice_c: You can almost always turn to miss an obstacle more quickly than you can stop
choice_d: Steering away from hazards only works below 20 mph
explanation: The manual states that stopping is not always the safest action in an emergency, and you can almost always turn to miss an obstacle more quickly than you can stop, though top-heavy vehicles and tractors with multiple trailers may flip over.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-33

question: Using the "stab braking" method described in the manual, how long can it take for the wheels to start rolling again after you release the brakes?
choice_a: Up to one second
choice_b: Up to five seconds
choice_d: The wheels never stop rolling with this method
explanation: The manual explains that with stab braking it can take up to one second for the wheels to start rolling after you release the brakes, and if you re-apply the brakes before they start rolling, the vehicle won't straighten out.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-34

question: According to the manual, what should you do immediately if a tire fails while driving?
choice_a: Brake hard right away to stop as quickly as possible
choice_b: Swerve sharply toward the shoulder
choice_d: Hold the steering wheel firmly and stay off the brake until the vehicle has slowed
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to hold the steering wheel firmly with both hands and stay off the brake until the vehicle has slowed down, then brake gently, pull off the road, and stop.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-35

question: Per the manual, the Department of Transportation requires ABS on truck tractors with air brakes built on or after what date?
choice_a: March 1, 1990
choice_b: March 1, 1997
choice_d: March 1, 2005
explanation: The manual states ABS is required on truck tractors with air brakes built on or after March 1, 1997, and on other air brake vehicles built on or after March 1, 1998.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-35

question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four causes of a skid listed in the manual?
choice_a: Over-braking
choice_b: Over-steering
choice_d: Under-inflated tires
explanation: The manual lists over-braking, over-steering, over-acceleration, and driving too fast for conditions as the four causes of a skid; under-inflated tires is not among them.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-36

question: What is the first step the manual recommends to correct a drive-wheel braking skid?
choice_a: Turn the steering wheel sharply in the opposite direction
choice_b: Stop braking, to let the rear wheels roll again
choice_d: Shift into a higher gear
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to stop braking first, which lets the rear wheels roll again and keeps them from sliding, and then counter-steer.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-37

question: What are the three basic steps the manual lists for any accident scene?
choice_a: Protect the area, notify authorities, care for the injured
choice_b: Call insurance, exchange information, file a report
choice_c: Move all vehicles immediately, take photos, wait for police
choice_d: Turn off engines, remove cargo, direct traffic
explanation: The manual lists the basic steps at any accident as: protect the area, notify authorities, and care for the injured.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-38

question: If your vehicle catches fire while en route and you need to pull off the road, what does the manual specifically say NOT to do?
choice_a: Notify emergency services of your location
choice_b: Pull into a service station
choice_c: Park in an open area away from buildings and trees
choice_d: Turn off the engine for an engine fire
explanation: The manual explicitly warns, "Don't pull into a service station!" when getting the vehicle off the road because of a fire.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-38

question: According to the manual, where should you aim a fire extinguisher when fighting a fire?
choice_a: Up into the flames
choice_b: At the source or base of the fire
choice_d: At the vehicle's fuel tank
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to aim the extinguisher at the source or base of the fire, not up into the flames, while staying as far away from the fire as possible.
source_note: Alaska CDL Manual (AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, rev. AK DMV 02/2018), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-39
